results.fact: Number of days
results.correct_value: A single long day for the route; the two-day figure belonged to one party's multi-objective trip.
results.evidence: The trip report behind the 'two-day' wording was a four-day weekend that linked the Liberty Bell traverse with this route, carrying 60-lb packs. The area page gives the south-face approach as 2.5-5 hours, i.e. a day outing from the hairpin.

patches.expect: A long, sustained day: the recorded ascent describes a grueling two-day effort involving multiple linked objectives, with heavy loads carried on the descent.
patches.value: A long, sustained day: multi-hour approach, three hard pitches that join the Kearney-Thomas finish, and a descent that can run long if you go looking for rappel anchors.

results.fact: Approach line: cross Early Winters Creek early vs stay west of it

The area page's south-face approach likewise follows the right side of the creek to a meadow (~40 min) and then heads left uphill for the low point on the ridge. The West Face approach is the one that cuts east across the creek early.

results.fact: Kangaroo Pass waypoint on the south-face approach
results.evidence: The Kangaroo Pass waypoint (1.3 mi, 6,671 ft) says the approach breaks east from the pass, while the approach prose and the area page turn left from the upper basin meadow toward the Big Kangaroo-Half Moon low point. A hiking report puts Kangaroo Pass about 3 miles from the hairpin, between the Early Winters and Twisp drainages, which does not fit a 1.3-mile pin. Not settled; no patch.

results.fact: Total elevation gain
results.correct_value: 3,166 ft car-to-summit (5,160 ft pullout to 8,326 ft summit)
results.evidence: The summit is 8,326 ft on the standard listing and the hairpin pullout is about 5,150 ft, so reaching the summit gains at least ~3,166 ft; gain_ft, the approach prose and both pins agree. The area page's ~2,800 ft is the approach gain to the face, not the summit day, so the itinerary day total is raised to match.

results.fact: Standard descent: rappel the face or not
results.correct_value: Standard descent is the notch-and-gully walk-down on one rope; rappelling the face (5-6 two-rope raps) is possible but loose and not recommended.
results.evidence: The route page gives the descent as scrambling to the summit notch and descending the gully to the hairpin, adding that rappelling the route takes 5-6 two-rope rappels from slings and trees and is not easy or safe. A trip report likewise descended the obvious gully back to the Hairpin Turn in about two hours. rope_note called the face rappel the published standard; corrected.

patches.expect: Lead on a single 60m rope. The published route description gives the standard descent as rappelling the face directly — 5-6 rappels using two ropes from a mix of slings and trees — so bring a second rope (tag line or a 2nd 60m) if you plan to descend that way rather than continue to the true summit. Multiple trip reports instead finish the extra pitch to the summit and walk off the standard gully descent back toward the Hairpin Turn (roughly 2 hours), which avoids needing a second rope at all — decide which descent option before racking up.
patches.value: Lead on a single 60m rope. The standard descent is not down the face: scramble to the notch and descend the gully back toward the Hairpin Turn (roughly 2 hours), which needs only the one rope. Rappelling the face itself is possible - 5-6 rappels using two ropes from a mix of slings and trees - but loose rock makes it slow and unsafe, so bring a second rope (tag line or a 2nd 60m) only if you deliberately plan that retreat.
patches.fact: Standard descent: rappel the face or not

results.fact: Wall aspect
results.evidence: One trip report calls the face southeast-facing, while the route page and the AAC report only name it the south face; the neighbouring Kearney-Thomas row stores SE. No two sources agree on an aspect, so neither aspect nor the schedule line is changed.

results.fact: Number and position of the corner pitches
results.evidence: The only description found (the first-ascent report) says the route traverses right to a big ledge, climbs two classic clean corners - the second through a 5.11c bulge - then slabs and easy cracks past a roof. That supports two corner pitches, making pitch_detail's third corner pitch (P3 5.10+) and its per-pitch grades doubtful, but no second independent source was found, so nothing is changed.

results.fact: Approach / round-trip distance
results.correct_value: About 2 mi (≈3.1 km) one-way, ~4 mi round trip
results.evidence: One trip report gives 3.8 mi round trip (5,160-8,280 ft); another gives about 4 mi round trip. That matches the waypoint chain (1.9 mi) and the itinerary (4 mi); dist_km held the miles figure as km, and the approach's '3 miles' is high.

results.fact: Car-to-car time
results.evidence: timing (7 h), the itinerary (6-8 h), the turnaround (5-6 h efficient, 8+ typical) and the approach (6+ h) agree; one trip report gives a 6-hour round trip. The 11.5 h in partner_requirements is the outlier.

results.fact: Where the roped climbing starts
results.correct_value: Rope up below the chockstone; the first pitch passes it to the notch, the second traverses around the summit block, the third is the 5.6 summit slab.
results.evidence: The route page's technical section passes under the distinctive chockstone in the shallow gully to the notch, then three short pitches (easy slab, traverse around the summit block, 5.6 slab). One trip report roped up below a large chockstone and climbed through a cannonhole at the gully's head; another roped up at the chockstone, with pitch 1 behind the chockstone to a rappel anchor, pitch 2 a ledge traverse and pitch 3 the summit slab.

patches.replace: Rope up below the chockstone: the first of the route's three roped pitches passes it to the notch, the second traverses around the summit block, and the third climbs the summit slab.

patches.expect: Class-3 slabs gain the ridge crest here; the low-5th-class pitches to the summit block begin from this notch.
patches.value: The first roped pitch, started below the chockstone, reaches the ridge crest at this notch; the second pitch traverses from here around the summit block.

patches.find: ARRIVAL AT THE ROPED CLIMBING: push past the chockstone and continue up class 3 slabs to A BROAD PLATFORM BELOW THE SUMMIT TOWER. That platform is where the route's three roped pitches begin. Flat ground below a tower, above a chockstone gully.

results.fact: Chockstone waypoint elevation vs a ~200 ft roped section
results.evidence: With roped climbing starting at the chockstone and totalling about 200 ft, the chockstone cannot sit at 7,400 ft below an 8,326 ft summit (the notch pin says 8,100). The true chockstone elevation was not found in any source, so the waypoint elevations are left alone.

results.correct_value: Three short pitches, about 200 ft in all
results.evidence: The route page gives three short pitches totalling about 200 ft (61 m). Two trip reports describe the roped pitches as short (a short class 4-5 pitch then the summit move; 'such a short pitch' and 'short'). detailed_rack is right; beta's ~500 ft/up to 4 pitches and pitch_detail's 150 m are wrong, so the invented per-pitch lengths are cleared rather than replaced.

results.fact: Total elevation gain
results.evidence: One trip report gives an elevation range of 5,160-8,280 ft (about 3,120 ft of gain); the route page says nearly 3,000 ft from the hairpin, and the 8,326 ft summit over the 5,160 ft pullout is ~3,166 ft. gain_ft (3,120) fits; the itinerary's 2,900 is low.

results.fact: Which side of the summit the approach gully leads to
results.evidence: The lower gully does head toward the crest south of the summit; around 7,500 ft a ramp leads left into the gully that reaches the notch north of the summit block, so the schedule describes the first leg and the approach the finish.

results.fact: Order of the creek crossing and the talus edge
results.evidence: The approach crosses at the talus edge after 0.5-0.7 mi; the waypoints cross at 0.4 mi and reach the talus fork at 0.9 mi. Sources only say to cut east across the creek (route page) or leave the path before the last large meadow about 0.7 mi out; none fixes the order of crossing and talus, so nothing is changed.

results.fact: Whether the descent gully needs a rope
results.evidence: The single rappel is from slung blocks at the notch, above the gully; the gully below it is descended on foot (one party rapped to their packs at the chockstone and then scree-surfed the gully). So 'a rope-free descent gully' and 'one rappel at the notch' describe different sections.

results.fact: Rappel anchor type
results.correct_value: The summit bolt is only used to lower/top-rope the leader; the rappel is from slung blocks at the notch.
results.evidence: The route page says to top-rope the leader down from a single rusty summit bolt and make a single rappel from two slung-block anchors at the notch. A trip report calls the summit bolt questionable and describes the rappel anchor separately.

patches.value: aging summit bolt used only to lower the leader
